channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Australian Politicians
item.description: Traces the long Australian tradition of despising, mocking and vigorously knocking politicians, from the nineteenth-century campaigns against Sir Henry Parkes and Graham Berry through the conscription battles of Billy Hughes, the de Groot bridge-cutting incident, and the unsparing treatment of Menzies, Gorton and McMahon.

item.title: Canberra
item.description: Surveys the long tradition of knocking Australia's purpose-built capital, from the 1909 naming competition through Robin Boyd's architectural verdict, the controversy over the $320,000 phallic fountain, and the $5 million artificial lake, charting how a city mocked as a sheep paddock and ghost town eventually learned to love itself.

item.title: The Sydney Opera House
item.description: A chronological compendium of knocks aimed at the Sydney Opera House from 1962 to 1971, from Noel Coward's 'Danish Blue' to Sir Tyrone Guthrie's 'mish-mash of buildings', tracing the battles with Joern Utzon, the steadily ballooning cost, and the running comparisons with Melbourne's own architectural failures.

item.title: The Beginning
item.description: Traces the Melbourne Cricket Club's beginnings in the rough settlement of 1838, its influential founders and the extraordinary duels fought by Peter Snodgrass, Redmond Barry and F. A. Powlett.

item.title: The First Cricket Matches
item.description: Follows the Melbourne Cricket Club's earliest contests, its lean years, the celebrations of Victoria's separation and the colony's first intercolonial matches against Van Diemen's Land.

item.title: A Cricket Selectors' Brawl
item.description: The 1912 Australian cricket selection crisis, in which Clem Hill punches fellow selector Peter McAlister during a stormy Sydney meeting, leaving McAlister with a black eye, reaches boiling point as the six greatest players in Australian cricket, including Hill, Armstrong, Trumper and Cotter, refuse to tour England under the disputed management arrangement.

item.title: Airliner Crashes in NE Victoria
item.description: The Australian National Airways Fokker tri-motor Southern Cloud, carrying six passengers and two crew on a flight from Sydney to Melbourne, vanishes somewhere over the storm-battered ranges of north-east Victoria in March 1931, prompting a massive aerial search led by Charles Kingsford Smith in the Southern Sun who searches for ten hours without result before declaring they must be found dead or alive.

item.title: An Incredible Colonial
item.description: John Pascoe Fawkner, one of Melbourne's founders and an extraordinarily self-made colonial figure, launches the Port Phillip Patriot and Melbourne Advertiser, a paper that attacks land sales favouring the rich over working men, despite Fawkner himself having been imprisoned, flogged, and constantly in legal strife through a life of unstoppable energy.

item.title: Annette Kellerman, the Perfect Woman
item.description: Annette Kellerman, the Sydney swimmer who wore steel leg braces as a child, won an American competition against 10,000 contestants as the 'perfect woman', dived into pools of crocodiles in New Zealand, starred in Hollywood films, and married her manager, returns to Sydney aboard the Orsova after ten years to lecture on physical fitness in six languages.

item.title: Brisbane Paralysed by General Strike
item.description: A general strike paralyses Brisbane in February 1912, with 34 unions out, shops and theatres closed, mounted police clashing with crowds in the streets, and Premier Denman appealing for volunteers after trouble began when the American superintendent of the tramway company sacked workers for wearing union badges on the job.

item.title: Canberra to be National Capital
item.description: Lady Denman opens a gold card-case and reads the name Canberra as the choice for Australia's national capital in March 1913, after years of debate in which the site ranged from the Snowy Mountains to a district King O'Malley said was so dry a crow would need to carry its water bags, while the public submitted names including Sydbourne, Thirstyville and the inspired Syd-Melb-Ad-Per-Bris-Ho.

item.title: Captain Armstrong 'Crucified'
item.description: The omission of Warwick Armstrong, the greatest all-rounder in cricket and the 'biggest boots in the game', from the NSW-Victoria match provokes his devoted admirer H.D. Westley to call a series of packed Indignation Meetings across Melbourne, while the MCG crowd keeps up an ironic chant to put Armstrong on as Patsy Hendren makes 271 for England.

item.title: Convicts Murder Inspector-General
item.description: John Price, Inspector-General of Penal Establishments, is stoned and battered to death by prisoners at Williamstown in March 1857 during a visit to hear complaints at the quarry works, after a prisoner named Kelly erupts over a refused ticket-of-leave application and the convicts, held in inhuman conditions on four prison hulks, attempt a mass breakout.

item.title: Dawn Fraser Expelled
item.description: Dawn Fraser, Australia's greatest swimmer, is expelled for ten years by the Australian Swimming Union following the Tokyo Olympics, along with three other girls given bans of three to four years, in sentences the entire swimming world regards as savage and without precedent for Olympic athletes, prompting both Dawn Fraser and Linda McGill to engage QCs and take legal action.

item.title: De Groot Opens Harbour Bridge
item.description: Captain Francis de Groot of the New Guard, craftily tacking on behind the Governor-General's military escort on horseback, slashes the opening ribbon of the Sydney Harbour Bridge with his sword moments before Premier Jack Lang can do so, shouting 'On behalf of decent and loyal citizens of New South Wales I now declare this bridge open', before being arrested and charged with being a person deemed to be insane.

item.title: Divorce in NSW
item.description: New South Wales passes the Matrimonial Clauses Bill in March 1874, allowing divorce on grounds of adultery, but with starkly different standards for men and women, in a parliamentary debate where opponents warn that allowing wives to prosecute husbands for adultery alone will open a very large door and overwhelm the barristers with work.

item.title: Embarking for the Boer War
item.description: The first battalion of the Federal Contingent sails from Woolloomooloo for South Africa aboard the Custodian in February 1900, with the occasion notably more subdued than the patriotic fervour of the first NSW contingent's departure in October 1899, and marred by a fatality when a private is dragged to his death by his bolting horse on the way to the wharf.

item.title: Ex-convict the Rothschild of Botany Bay
item.description: Sydney buries Samuel Terry, the 'Rothschild of Botany Bay', in the grandest funeral in the colony's history, a man who arrived in 1801 as a convict sentenced for stealing 400 pairs of stockings and died in 1838 worth over half a million pounds, having been innkeeper, stonemason, farmer, banker and the principal benefactor of the Sydney Public School.

item.title: Farewell to Dame Nellie Melba
item.description: Dame Nellie Melba dies in February 1931 at St Vincent's Hospital in Sydney and is borne back to Melbourne by a special funeral train that stops at every country platform along the route, where crowds who had never seen her alive kneel at the coffin, before she is buried at Lilydale beside her parents.

item.title: Gaslight for Hobart
item.description: Liverpool Street Hobart witnesses its first gas lighting in March 1852, with the Hobart Mercury publishing careful instructions for residents on how to operate the new gas taps without shattering their glass chimneys, while Alderman Thomson notes the 180 new street lamps are actually cheaper than Sydney's gas and infinitely cheaper than Melbourne's.

item.title: General Gordon and Khartoum Fall to the Mahdi
item.description: News reaches Australia that General Charles Gordon has been killed at Khartoum after a year-long siege by Sudanese rebel forces, provoking a grief and fury in the colonies unmatched since the death of the Duke of Wellington, with much of the anger directed at the Gladstone government's dilly-dallying, and New South Wales Premier William Dalley cabling London to offer troops without waiting for Parliament's approval.

item.title: General MacArthur Arrives
item.description: General Douglas MacArthur arrives in Melbourne as Supreme Allied Commander in the South-West Pacific in March 1942, fresh from a dramatic dash through Japanese defences from Bataan in twelve PT boats, to give his first press conference and announce he will fight to get the maximum out of Australia's war situation, as new manpower regulations requiring all citizens to register and carry identity cards come into force.

item.title: Hinkler 'The New Lindbergh'
item.description: Bert Hinkler completes the first solo flight from England to Australia in 15 and a half days, arriving in Darwin in a tiny Avro Avian biplane to 400 telegrams and a bottle of beer despite the city's beer strike, before flying on to Bundaberg where the entire town is taking a holiday and church bells will ring when he passes overhead.

item.title: HMAS Perth and Yarra Lost
item.description: Prime Minister Curtin announces that HMAS Perth and HMAS Yarra must be presumed lost in the Java Sea following the fiercest naval engagement since Jutland, fought at suicidal odds in the final desperate defence before the fall of Java, with 16,744 officers and men unaccounted for out of a total Australian force of 17,031.

item.title: Japanese Bomb Darwin
item.description: Japanese aircraft launch a devastating surprise attack on Darwin on 19 February 1942, the first and largest foreign attack on Australian soil, with 188 aircraft sinking eight ships, killing 243 people, destroying the post office and many key installations, and forcing the evacuation of a ghost town in what Curtin describes as Australia's first battle.

item.title: Knuckled Fighters Take to the Bush
item.description: Australian champion Larry Foley meets American challenger Abe Hickin in a bare-knuckle contest staged in a red-gum glade near Echuca on the NSW-Victoria border, after elaborate attempts to evade police forces of both colonies, with Foley's scientific boxing so completely mastering Hickin's bar-room brawling that a very tall dark bearded man, possibly Ned Kelly, comes up to congratulate the winner.

item.title: Last Ride for Captain Moonlite
item.description: George Scott, alias Captain Moonlite, is hanged at Darlinghurst Jail alongside accomplice Thomas Rogan for the Wantabadgery station siege, which followed Scott's earlier career of bank robbery, a stint in Pentridge, public lectures on prison reform, and the adoption of his notorious alias after a bank manager recognised his voice mid-robbery.

item.title: Lola Montez Horse-whips Editor
item.description: Lola Montez, the notorious Irish-born dancer whose Spider Dance has scandalised Ballarat's Diggers and the Argus alike, horse-whips the editor of the Ballarat Times after he publishes an attack on her morals under the pseudonym 'Civis', only for Seekamp to arrive at her hotel with his own horsewhip and the confrontation to nearly end in a pistol duel.

item.title: Mace Disappears during Drunken Freak
item.description: The ceremonial gold mace of Victoria's Legislative Assembly vanishes from its oak box in October 1892, and a year of rumour culminates in the Ballarat Courier alleging it has been kept in a Melbourne brothel and used in travesties of parliamentary procedure, forcing the paper's proprietor before the bar of the House.

item.title: Mad Jack Berry
item.description: Victoria's Premier Graham Berry earns the nickname 'Mad Jack Berry' after sacking 278 public servants in a single day, a drastic response to the Legislative Council's rejection of his bill to pay members of Parliament three hundred pounds a year.
